newsitem.title: USA: NHTSA probes Subaru air bags, Ford, GM trucks.
newsitem.headline: NHTSA probes Subaru air bags, Ford, GM trucks.

text.p: The federal govenment's auto safety agency said Friday it was investigating inadvertent air bag deployment on two Subaru car models and steering problems affecting Ford Motor Co. and General Motors Corp. trucks.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, also said in its monthly defect investigation report that it has received seven reports of air bags deploying in 1995 Subaru Impreza and Legacy models without crashes, resutling in two crashes and seven injuries.

Complaints of "oversensitive" air bag deployment on the Legacy occurred after the underside of the car scraped the road, ran over a dip in the road, hit a pot hole or got stuck in a ditch in snow. Two complaints on the Impreza model reported that the air bag allegedly deployed after the brakes were applied.
"The air bag is clearly not supposed to go off if there's no crash," said NHTSA spokesman Tim Hurd. "That's why we're looking into this."

There are about 99,000 1995 Subaru Imprezas and Legacys on the road. A spokesman for Cherry Hill, N.J.-based Subaru of America Inc., a unit of Fuji Heavy Industries Ltd., was not immediately available for comment.

The probe comes as the NHTSA has been deluged with consumer requests to disconnect air bags over fears that their explosive force can kill children and small women. The deaths of about 35 children and 20 adults have been attributed to air bags, which inflate at speeds up to 200 miles per hour.
Some of the deaths, which have included decapitations of infants and toddlers, have allegedly been caused in extremely low-speed crashes, such as parking lot fender-benders.
Hurd said the NHTSA had no standard trigger speed for air bag deployment, but required that vehicles pass a barrier crash test at 30 miles per hour in which the air bags protect unbelted adults.

NHTSA has proposed reducing the inflation power of future air bags by 20 percent to 35 percent and allowing consumers to disconnect them as a stop-gap measure before the industry can introduce so-called smart air bags that detect the size and position of occupants and adjust inflation pressures accordingly.
Automakers want the lower-power bags, but oppose the disconnections.

In other probes opened in December, NHTSA said it is investigating the lock-up of power steering systems in Ford 1992-1995 model E-150 Econoline vans, and in Ford 1992 model B-700 medium-duty trucks, school buses and truck chassis.

The B-700 probe involves steering lockup due to a loss or significant reduction in power steering assist. In one instance, the steering locked up on a school bus carrying whitewater rafters, causing it to hit a guard rail and several trees, the agency said. One person was injured in the crash.

In the Econoline probe, five owners complained that steering lockup occurred when applying the brakes and attempting to manoeuvre the vehicle at low speeds. No accidents or injuries associated with the problem were reported.

In another Ford truck probe, NHTSA said it was investigating complaints of spontaneous shattering of glass sunroofs in 1992-93 model Explorer sport utility vehicles. The problem, which has resulted in two injuries involving minor cuts, may affect up to 118,000 vehicles.
A Ford spokeswoman said the automaker was cooperating with the probes.

The NHTSA also said it is investigating GM's 1996-model C/K-series trucks, including pickup trucks, sport utility vehicles and cab-chassis for a loss of steering control caused by a coupling bolt falling out of the steering column.

The agency said that it had three reports of the problem, resulting in one accident that caused two injuries. NHTSA had previously investigated the identical problem in 1995-model GM C/K trucks, but closed it because it did not have enough evidence to identify a defect.
The number of vehicles involved in the GM and Ford steering-related probes was not immediately available.
